rv.q: The play in turn makes us care for them, out there in all their recklessness on the edge of the night.
It’s lively and funny, but it doesn’t reimagine the film or fully recreate its propulsive energy.
But they have to fight through too much else for attention.
Once the romance between Sonny and his lover, Leon (Esteban Andres Cruz), becomes the focus, the play takes an abrupt turn that is unconvincing.
The film updates “Afternoon” to an awareness of this union and what it means that’s more upfront and unapologetic and, in its way, more sentimental.
For a play about a real-life 1972 bank robbery and hostage situation, the stakes are curiously medium, as if everything will magically return to normal on next week’s episode.

Though it would have been a riskier proposition, maybe an updated Afternoon actually set in 2026 would have made better use of this cast than a play that attempts an awkward negotiation between 1970s period details and a 2020s sensibilities.
But none of them can save what is otherwise a hollow and desultory maladaptation.
But there’s no getting around the fact that this undercooked staging does feel like the product of an unresolved artistic dispute.
But the creators behind the new Broadway production of Afternoon seem to have gotten stuck on the funny part.
Sadly, I’m obliged to report a tragic pileup on the Belt Parkway.
The comedy is so broad under Rupert Goold’s direction that the central drama — will any of these hostages, much less the two bank robbers, come out alive? — is almost beside the point.
Indeed, it’s the little one-on-one pictures – rather than the bigger one – that make this “Afternoon” time well spent, flaws and all.
In the end, the new Afternoon is a mostly satisfying experience that offers impressive big production values.
This piece suffers mightily from inconsistency.
Afternoon rolls over when it should bite.
In its general inclination for overstatement, though, this “Afternoon” feels very contemporary.
It’s essentially Disney for Dads, a curious blend of head-patting nostalgia and earnest artistry, delivered with a refreshing lack of cynicism.
And while it may be unfair to compare them, those of us who know the film well are likely to feel the play falls short of expectations.
The moment ironically served to demonstrate that this Afternoon ultimately feels like a musicalization of the film minus the musical numbers.
But I guess nobody can, because Guirgis hasn’t.
As a piece of theater, it feels less like a reimagining than a repackaging — a familiar property pressed into service as a showcase for recognizable television talent.

But this high-prestige vehicle is an in-between affair, unable to live up to the cinematic dazzle of its source material yet never finding its own identity as an alternate version of its stranger-than-fiction true story.
Now, this ultimately tragic story of two desperate bunglers comes off as a sitcom with almost zero dramatic tension or suspense.
Deprived of its fidgety tension, this Afternoon isn’t so much a slow burn as a slow melt.
An appalling near-disaster that fundamentally misunderstands everything that makes the film so unnervingly devastating.
It is engaging, memorable, and stirring—maybe not in the exact same ways as the film.
Everything old is, indeed, new again and my audience ate it up.
But the sitcom bones and stereotypes keep it from being the classic it wants to be.
Afternoon has two of TV's best and one of Broadway's most inventive sets, but this stage adaptation can't hold the room hostage long enough.
A play about queer survival that doesn't reckon with how much more precarious that survival has become isn't radical. It's nostalgia.
Guirgis’s understandable efforts to turn Frank Pierson’s Oscar-winning screenplay into a visceral theatrical experience repeatedly fall short.
Guirgis and Goold have gone where most adapters refuse to—presenting purely their own thing with no apologies. Cue applause.

But to my surprise, I had a pretty good time.Maybe that's a result of expectations. Sidney Lumet’s movie and its iconic performances by Al Pacino and John Cazale have been beloved by generations of moviegoers (including me) and what seems to have most disappointed the people who don’t like the staged version is that it’s different from the film.
Sadly, for me, the play was an exhausting drag.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this star-driven adaptation, with many finding it tonally confused and unable to justify its existence beyond the film. While some praise Bernthal's performance and Guirgis's New York voices, most fault the uneven mix of comedy and drama.

vs.sum: The August Wilson Theatre offers good sightlines from most seats, although the rake isn't steep, which can cause issues if seated behind taller patrons. The theater has average comfort with decent legroom but tight seats. Its Italian-inspired design and cozy feel enhance the ambiance, making it a pleasant venue overall. Facilities are adequate, with standard amenities and helpful staff.

acc.note: Stair lift to orchestra; elevator between orchestra and mezzanine. Infrared headsets available.

vr.q: This was an imperfect but very engaging night in the theater. I really enjoyed the play and I really enjoyed the performances.
Regardless, I ended up really enjoying this show — it had to grow on me, but I can see why the film is a classic, being a comedy thriller with anti-establishment messaging.
It may not be perfect, but it works.

I mostly enjoyed the experience of watching it, but I was vaguely aware that word of mouth from the theatre community was kind of negative. So the very next day I rewatched the film... and unfortunately the side by side comparison forced me to acknowledge that a lot of the criticisms were spot on.
